thread.title: Gain Exposure To Apple Through Berkshire Hathaway - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Eric Nickolaison
title: Gain Exposure To Apple Through Berkshire Hathaway - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

organizations.name: apple through berkshire hathaway - apple inc.

text:
I thought it would be prudent to understand Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and the state of its economic moat, as I'm basically long AAPL through Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK.A ) (NYSE: BRK.B ).
Moat Analysis There's an interesting dynamic occurring at Apple. The company has thrived off of its economic moat of high switching costs and intangible assets over the past decade. It controls the user experience that offers a wide array of utilities at the customers' finger tips. A disciplinary moat is at play, and I have discussed what this means at length here . Basically, the moat stems from the company controlling the environment for the consumer and how they interact with its products or services. Management's ability to bring hardware and software together in such an integrated design was the source of this. But it has been making an extension into a different type of competitive advantage.
Quite a few years have passed since the first smartphones were introduced. Now consumers have many options within this category, so I'm not sure Apple's iPhone is superior anymore. It still has sticky features like the iCloud service, App Store, iTunes, FaceTime, etc. All features could convince a person from switching. In addition, the company offers many auxiliary products such as iPad, Apple Watch, etc. that provide a wonderful ecosystem with having all devices seamlessly connected.
All of these sound great, but still why has Apple been able to take such large amounts of profits within a competitive industry?
First, it's built up a large user base because of the reasons stated above, which has almost created this tribal-like group. Now, over the last 2-3 years, it has been leveraging its brand/switching costs against the user base to increase prices. Management's ability on narration is top-notch, creating this perception that Apple products should be in the realm of a luxury good was brilliant. I would bet most people have been asked what phone you have or what iPhone you have. It's like the type of phone a person has shows their social status, and if you don't have the latest and greatest, you're at the bottom.
Average selling prices have significantly increased these past two years. Apple's iPhone is the most valuable since colleagues and friends admire or are almost jealous of the person with the latest release. I think this comment is especially true for the younger demographic.
In my opinion, pricing is probably reaching its peak now. A sign of this is when Apple announced it will no longer be releasing unit sales numbers anymore. Any Apple investor should be discouraged with this decision. I understand some of the rationale behind it, as revenue growth and iPhone unit growth used to be highly correlated, but have diverged recently as revenue growth is outpacing unit growth with pricing increases. Management taking away the visibility of iPhone unit growth was a way of saying unit numbers will probably be flat or fluctuate extremely. It's trying to control the narrative of the company's performance.
A key aspect on how management is leveraging its brand is through its retail stores. It has slick designs coupled with thinking differently. It's a place for consumers to hang out and learn. It has really flipped the retail model upside down and added an upscale model.
Investors can gain exposure to Apple through a more diversified way. All you have to do is buy Berkshire Hathaway. In the last five years, Apple has earned $289 billion in free cash flow, while returning $212 billion in buybacks, reducing the share count by 18.3%. All of this occurring while maintaining over a $100 billion net cash position. Moving forward, even if the company generates $60 billion a year in free cash flow, this equates to an 8.5% cash flow yield against enterprise value, an attractive yield for a company that I would say has a strong moat. By contemplating what Buffett's thoughts are, I would bet he is almost certain that he'll own a larger part of the business in the future through the company's buybacks, a capital allocation method that he loves when the equity is undervalued or fairly valued.
Under very static assumptions on free cash flow, and a few ticks upwards on the multiple, provides decent returns for shareholders over the next five years. With high cash flow visibility and a management team willing to allocate cash to buybacks, I've modeled a valuation scenario taking buybacks into account. Within the model, I assume cash flow to be flat, $14 million in capex (historical average), and dividends creeping up just a little to $15 billion annually. All cash flow leftover is applied towards share repurchases.

The 8% return doesn't take into consideration the roughly 2% dividend yield, pushing up the return to 10%. Even at an 18x free cash multiple equates to a 6% yield. Still quite attractive for a company that has a massive pile of cash. The model doesn't even take into consideration this pile of cash. Management could continue to leverage this to enhance returns. Berkshire Hathaway roughly owns 5% of the company currently. Under the model, data points to Berkshire owning almost 6% of the company if it continues to hold 252 million shares at the end of five years.
In addition, some quant investors have been highlighting firms that buy back large percentages of their shares outperform the market, especially the high-conviction repurchasers. This means large percentages of the shares outstanding are decreasing at a good pace. Maybe Warren Buffett is a quant investor who only has to use his head to calculate data, instead of algorithms.
